description: "Vista Oculta" focuses on planetary topography and AI orchestration. We are building an auditable CAD engine that processes digital elevation models (Earth, Moon, Mars) with mathematical error margins and hashed logs. We aim to demonstrate advanced AI agent orchestration to find planetary analogs. If you have skills in planetary geology, GIS, UI/UX, or storytelling for a killer 30s pitch, join us to build verifiable science for Space Apps and LPSC!
summary:
We screened 5.1 million land pixels (0.05°) by how bare ground heats and cools using NASA MODIS skin temperature, albedo, and emissivity, keeping sites whose relief also resembles Jezero crater on Mars or the lunar south pole.

In a pre-registered blind test, the frozen method ranked 11 unseen analogs above 45 land regions 87 % of the time (AUC 0.873; bar 0.80). A larger pre-registered test (143 literature analogs vs. 150 regions) failed: AUC 0.67 (95 % CI 0.60–0.73). It detects arid, Jezero-like terrain above chance, not impact craters (0.58), ice, or caves. Both results remain on record.

Unprompted, it rediscovered Qaidam Basin and the Namib, and flagged two non-obvious candidates: Sudan's Nubian Desert and the unstudied Saudi side of Wadi Rum.

Each candidate card quantifies similarity, failure modes, and rover mobility. In our Mission Console, onboard sensing cuts steep-cell (>24°) incidents from 11 to 2 of 45 traverses and quantifies how much of a Mars drive an Earth test represents (95–100 % median; 73–88 % worst case). A sealed Gale crater test showed orbital maps can sit 240–330 m off, causing 16 % detour energy waste versus only 4 % saved by energy-optimal routing on known terrain. Every number traces to a hash-chained log.
details:
Direct project links (no login required):

- Interactive Project Page: https://wmeur385-cpu.github.io/hidden/

- Mission Console (offline 3D web app with onboard sensing, terramechanics & HUD): https://wmeur385-cpu.github.io/hidden/console.html

- Rover Explorer (3D 5-stop mission simulator): https://wmeur385-cpu.github.io/hidden/explorer.html

- 7-Slide Overview (PDF): https://wmeur385-cpu.github.io/hidden/slides/hidden_view_slides.pdf

- Product One-Pager & API Sketch (PDF): https://wmeur385-cpu.github.io/hidden/product/hidden_view_onepager.pdf

- Source Code, Data & Hash-Chained Log (GitHub): https://github.com/wmeur385-cpu/hidden

What it does. The page combines four parts into candidate cards:

- a global map of ground behaviour;

- a relief test against Moon and Mars targets;

- a model that separates the ground from the air;

- an interactive rover navigability map, where a rover drives the lowest-risk route;

- the Mission Console, one offline web app that joins the analog world map with a rover mission that senses the ground on board, replans, feels the soil (slip, sinkage, tip-over margin in Mars, Earth or Moon gravity) and flies a fighter-style HUD;

- the Rover Explorer, a 3D simulator of the five candidates. It runs an exploration mission to 5 science stops in the lowest-risk order, with live pitch and roll, a route profile and click-to-drive re-planning under the same rule.

Each card answers the four questions of the challenge: what is similar, to what degree, where the analogy fails, and how the site helps exploration.

How it works.

1. Ground behaviour. We used three MODIS measurements, rank-averaged with fixed weights, in each hemisphere's summer month of 2025:

- the day–night swing of Aqua skin temperature (~14:30 vs ~02:30 local time);

- apparent thermal inertia, (1 − albedo)/swing, with MCD43C3 albedo;

- 8.5 µm emissivity.

2. Relief. Every elevation model was averaged to a common 200 m grid: Earth, LRO LOLA for the Moon, HRSC–MOLA for Mars. Each 20 km window gets five slope and relief statistics. We then measure the Mahalanobis distance to the target's own windows.

3. Ground vs air. A layered soil model exchanges heat with measured air (NASA POWER). It was calibrated in July 2025 and judged in January 2025 against MODIS.

- In deserts, treating air temperature as if it were the ground errs by 3–12 K on average; the model errs by 1.2–1.8 K.

- On the Moon, with the air switched off, it gives 94–385 K at the equator. LRO Diviner measured about 95 K and 387–397 K.

4. Rover navigability. We used Copernicus 30 m relief and 40 Monte Carlo terrains to map, cell by cell, the chance of a slope over 15° (nominal) and over 24° (current Perseverance maximum). A lowest-risk route is drawn on top. On the page, a rover drives that route while a ghost rover tries the straight line. At Qaidam the route is 8.1 km instead of 6.3 km, but it avoids 98 % of the steep ground; the ghost stops at 5.8 km, where a slope over 24° becomes more likely than not.

Validation. Pass criteria were written before each run.

- On the development set (8 analogs, 45 unlabeled regions), ground behaviour alone failed (AUC 0.795) and the cascade reached 0.939. But the cascade had been designed after seeing that data.

- An independent reviewer agent flagged this. So, before looking, we logged a new test: 11 new analog sites, 45 new regions, method frozen, bar 0.80.

- It passed with AUC 0.873 (95 % interval 0.77–0.95). Combining the two layers beat each one alone.

- A larger pre-registered blind test (143 literature analogs from catalogues and Crossref-checked papers, coordinates from Wikidata/OpenStreetMap; 150 new regions, seed 20261116; same frozen code) failed both bars: AUC 0.666, 95 % CI 0.600–0.727 (bars: 0.80, and lower CI end >= 0.70). Relief alone 0.65, ground behaviour alone 0.60. By analog type: Apollo training and simulant-source sites 0.74, fluvial 0.74, hydrothermal 0.73, volcanic 0.64, evaporite/desert 0.62, impact 0.58, ice 0.42. The 0.873 rested on 11 mostly arid, famous sites; it does not generalize. We retract it as a general claim.

- The reviewer re-derived 8 key numbers from raw data. The relief ranking was re-run four times with identical raw-data hashes and results.

- Then we attacked our own result. We rebuilt the method in all 1,458 reasonable variants of 7 choices (sensor, thermal layers, season, percentile, box size, relief weight, combination rule), screened them with a Taguchi L18 orthogonal array and a response surface, and judged nothing on the blind set. 76 % of the variants pass the 0.80 bar (median 0.855).

- The weakest choice is the season: with the winter month the blind AUC drops to 0.79.

- Tuning on the development set did not transfer (blind 0.865), so the method stays frozen.

- Two new random sets of 45 regions give 0.875 and 0.865, and shifting the test coordinates by up to 30 km never drops the AUC below 0.846.

Onboard sensing and terramechanics (Mission Console). The self-destruction round showed that a planner tuned on orbital data still steps on terrain over 24°: the missing piece is information. So the rover now senses the ground: a lidar/stereo-class sensor on a mast (acoustic sonar is useless in a vacuum and in thin Martian air), line of sight traced on the real terrain, each range fused into the rover's own map, and replanning when new risk appears. Everything was pre-registered in the notebook and judged on the 30 m answer key, 45 traverses per rule (5 sites × 9 orbit conditions).

- With onboard sensing (frozen default) the route above 15° falls from 4.9 % to 1.1 %, and the loss falls from 0.066 to 0.022.

- With a configuration frozen before running, 2 of 45 traverses still touched a cell steeper than 24° (orbit-only: 11), so our pre-registered zero criterion failed. A second pre-registered rule, 'verify before forbidding', judged on 45 unseen runs, removed all refusals and cut the loss from 0.034 to 0.013 but still left 3 of 45. A third rule, 'a slope counts only when the cell and its four neighbours were ranged', brought steep cells to 0 of 45 on another unseen set, but only by trapping the rover at convex crests: 28 of 45 traverses ended without reaching the goal. It failed too, and the thread stopped there, as pre-registered: at 30 m, the last steep cells and mobility trade against each other.

- A Taguchi L18 × L9 design over eight sensor and planner factors shows the replanning interval and the sensor range matter most. Paired over the 45 traverses, the sensor lowers the loss in 29, raises it in 4 and ties in 12 (Wilcoxon p = 4 × 10^-5), but the runs share only five terrains, and the sensor ranges the 30 m answer key itself (its best case). The frozen default's two misses were 24.5° and 25.2° cells.

- The simulator in the browser was run in Node on the embedded data and matched the Python reference cell by cell (295 steps, 12,018 ranges, same seed).

- Terramechanics (Bekker–Wong rigid wheel, Curiosity class; soil stiffness scaled with gravity after Wong 2012; low-gravity traction loss from parabolic flights, Niksirat et al. 2020; 2,000 draws over three literature soils, one quoted from a textbook table still to be checked): median maximum slope at <=20 % slip on loose soil, Mars 5.0°, Earth with a Mars-weight test rover 5.1°, Earth full mass 5.2°.

- How much of Mars an Earth test represents, cell by cell, on the five sites: a Mars-weight test rover gives the same drive/no-drive verdict as Mars on 95–100 % of the terrain in the median case and 73–88 % in the worst 5 % of soils; a full-mass rover gives 96–100 % and 84–91 %. The Mars-weight test rover has the worst worst case (under 1 g the soil is stiffer for the same wheel load); the full-mass rover errs slightly more often but by less. On bare rock, gravity cancels.

- Rigor battery (rigor.py, recomputed from the run files). Calibration of the orbit map over 1.8 million cells: Brier skill 0.41 and ECE 0.009 for P(>24°), but 51 % of the truly steep cells sit at P≈0 and predictions of 1–10 % come true 20–24 % of the time, which is why no threshold on orbital data can be enough. The sensing gain survives resampling whole terrains (loss −0.043, 95 % CI 0.018–0.074) and a mixed model with terrain as a random effect (p = 0.009); the effective sample size is five terrains. Leaving one terrain out, a re-tuned rule beats the frozen default on 3 of 5 held-out terrains and loses on 1, so the default is not over-fitted. Sobol indices say the Earth-vs-Mars gap is driven by the sinkage exponent n (total index 0.41) and cohesion (0.24): measure those first in the field. Latin hypercube sampling gives the same precision as plain Monte Carlo with about 13× fewer draws.

- Darwinian cycle, sealed on real Mars (ciclo_rover/). The AI wrote one candidate driving rule per generation and a frozen judge scored it (SHA-256 of judge and problem recorded before generation 1, identical at the end). Tuning on Qaidam, Namib and An Nafud; validation on NW Saudi and Nubian (seen in earlier rounds with other seeds); sealed test on Jezero crater, Mars: the HiRISE 1 m terrain model made for Perseverance's landing (USGS Mars 2020 TRN) averaged to 30 m as truth, and the real HRSC–MOLA 200 m map as the orbital prior. The target, written before running, was half the frozen default's validation loss (0.0090); generation 3 reached 0.0089. Opened once, Mars gave 0.0055, against 0.0075 for the frozen rule and 0.0223 orbit-only. On Mars, 2 of 8 runs (the same traverse, two noise seeds) still crossed one cell of about 26°, as every rule did. On the Earth validation terrains, runs touching a >24° cell fell from 3 to 1 of 18, but routes were 39 % longer than ideal on average (frozen rule: 9 %), up to 2.5×, because the pre-registered loss does not charge distance (flagged before looking). One of three random-parameter controls matched the evolved rule on validation; the gain comes from one factor, the weight on 15° risk, and we do not credit the AI search over random search.

- Energy: does the path of least resistance save battery? (energia.py, ciclo_energia/, auditoria_prior.py). We added watt-hours to the same Bekker–Wong wheel, with a Curiosity-class power budget taken from sources (899 kg, 4 cm/s, 150 W base load, 2 × 42 Ah batteries, MMRTG about 114 W ≈ 2.8 kWh per sol; 28 V and a 50 % drive efficiency are assumptions). The model gives 1.52 Wh per metre on the flat, inside the 1.04–3.47 Wh/m band implied by the published 150–500 W at 4 cm/s, and 23° as the steepest climb the wheels can make. Three findings. (1) With the terrain known, the least-energy route is only 3.9 % cheaper than the shortest safe route, on Earth analogs and on Gale alike: on a slow rover the base load dominates, so energy ≈ time ≈ distance. (2) The waste is detours forced by not knowing the terrain: the sensing rover spent 16 % more than the least-energy route on average, 57 % in the worst case. (3) A second darwinian cycle, sealed on Gale crater (Curiosity's terrain, MSL 1 m DEM, never used before), tried to plan on watt-hours: none of the AI's mutations beat the safety rule (planning on watt-hours over the blurry orbital relief was 26 % worse), and random-parameter draws from the same family did no worse (two scored better on validation, all three worse on tuning; the spread is about ±0.04), so the AI search gets no credit and there is no evidence that blending energy into distance helps. Opened once, Gale broke the rule: loss 0.61 against 0.19 on Earth. After the seal we found why: the real HRSC–MOLA map sits 240–330 m south of the MSL relief (94 m of that was our own window-cropping bug, now fixed and covered by a test), and the rover believed the map erred by 2 m when it erred by 15–32 m. Co-registering the map, a pre-registered fix, cut the loss to 0.34 (on the landing plain from 0.71 to 0.18) but missed its own bar of 0.25, because on Mount Sharp's foothills every rule, and the orbit-only plan, still met a climb steeper than the wheels can take: the safety rule looks at cell slope, not at the climb limit along the step. That is the next fix, not yet tested. The Mission Console now shows the watt-hours, battery and sols of every drive against the least-energy route on the truth.

- Cinema camera. The console now renders the rover to scale with a shadow map cast by the sun of the actual Sentinel-2 acquisition, environment reflections from the same sky model, wheel tracks, ranging beams to the cells the sensor really measured, and dust that falls under the chosen gravity (pure ballistic arcs on the Moon). The ground near the rover is the real 30 m data; no sand ripples or rocks were invented.

- The Mission Console shows all of it in one offline page: the analog world map on the NASA Blue Marble mosaic, the rover on Sentinel-2 imagery draped on 30 m terrain, live lidar returns, the rover's belief map against the answer key, a fighter-style HUD, and gravity and soil switches.

The Moon, shown with NASA data. The relief test reads LRO LOLA 118 m elevation; the slides show it as shaded relief (polar stereographic within 100 km of the south pole, with Shackleton, and the Apollo 17 valley at Taurus-Littrow). Teide (Canary Islands) is the closest Earth relief window for both lunar targets (distance 1.59 to the south polar region, compatible <= 3.1; 1.38 to Taurus-Littrow, compatible <= 2.3), followed by Puna / Ojos del Salado and the Antarctic Dry Valleys. Relief only: no Earth site has the Moon's vacuum, gravity or ~290 K daily swing.

Where the analogy fails. Earth cannot reproduce:

- reduced gravity (0.17 g, 0.38 g);

- the lunar vacuum or Mars' ~0.6 kPa atmosphere;

- the radiation environment;

- the size of the lunar daily temperature swing (about 290 K, against 30–41 K on our candidates).

Each card adds site-specific failures, such as wind-made dunes standing in for impact-made relief.

What failed and stays on record.

- The larger blind test (143 literature analogs) failed: AUC 0.67. Not a general analog detector.

- The energy cycle missed its target, and the AI's mutations did no better than random draws.

- Sealed on Gale crater, the driving rule broke (0.61); part of it was our own map-cropping bug, now fixed with a test.

- Richer relief features did worse than the simple ones.

- Ground behaviour alone failed its bar.

- The development test was not blind.

- Relief alone dropped to 0.72 on new analogs.

- The MODIS 8.5 µm emissivity turned out to be a table value.

- Polar summer has no night pass.

- The 200 m grid hides steep ground that a rover would feel.

- Rover plans made from orbit-like data (30–180 m, 1–6 m error) step on at least one cell over 24° in 16 of 45 cases when judged on the 30 m terrain (Monte Carlo risk estimator; the closed-form estimator used in the sensing experiments gives 11 of 45 on the same conditions). Tuning the planner does not fix it; the rover has to sense the ground ahead.

Why it matters. Analog sites are often chosen for logistics and visual resemblance. This gives a systematic, global and auditable way to find and rank new sites, and to say honestly how far each one is from the real thing.

Tools. Python, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, rasterio, pyhdf, shapely, matplotlib, Pillow and ffmpeg. All code is open source under Apache-2.0.

Prior work, declared. Two general tools were written before the hackathon: the terrain-reading engine (terreno_folha.py, October 2026) and the hash-chained notebook (orquestra.py). Everything specific to this challenge was built from 11 November 2026 on, after the challenge statements were published; each step has a timestamp in the notebook. That covers the relief test against Moon and Mars, the ground-behaviour screen, the ground/air model, the cascade, the blind test, the rover check, the page and the video.
